(a) In General.—Subject to subsection (b), the Council, acting through the Office of Financial Research, may require a bank holding company with total consolidated assets of $50,000,000,000 or greater or a nonbank financial company supervised by the Board of Governors, and any subsidiary thereof, to submit certified reports to keep the Council informed as to—
        (1) the financial condition of the company; 
        (2) systems for monitoring and controlling financial, operating, and other risks; 
        (3) transactions with any subsidiary that is a depository institution; and 
        (4) the extent to which the activities and operations of the company and any subsidiary thereof, could, under adverse circumstances, have the potential to disrupt financial markets or affect the overall financial stability of the United States.  
    (b) Use of Existing Reports.—
        (1) In general.—For purposes of compliance with subsection (a), the Council, acting through the Office of Financial Research, shall, to the fullest extent possible, use—
            (A) reports that a bank holding company, nonbank financial company supervised by the Board of Governors, or any functionally regulated subsidiary of such company has been required to provide to other Federal or State regulatory agencies or to a relevant foreign supervisory authority; 
            (B) information that is otherwise required to be reported publicly; and 
            (C) externally audited financial statements.  
        (2) Availability.—Each bank holding company described in subsection (a) and nonbank financial company supervised by the Board of Governors, and any subsidiary thereof, shall provide to the Council, at the request of the Council, copies of all reports referred to in paragraph (1). 
        (3) Confidentiality.—The Council shall maintain the confidentiality of the reports obtained under subsection (a) and paragraph (1)(A) of this subsection.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that outside companies supply information to a federal body, and that State and foreign regulators are mentioned, so outsiders are involved. But this is a compulsory reporting obligation imposed on regulated firms, not consultation with them before a federal decision. The State and foreign regulators appear only as sources of existing reports the Council should reuse. Nothing here provides for rulemaking, public comment, a hearing, an advisory body, or a right to sue.

opus.w: This section lets the Council make regulated companies submit certified reports about their financial condition and risk controls. That is compelled supervisory disclosure, not outside parties weighing in on a federal decision. The tempting reading treats any private-to-government communication as participation, but the companies have no consultative, advisory, comment, hearing, or legal-challenge role. Using existing reports and keeping them confidential are likewise internal data-handling rules.

opus.b: The tempting reading is that this is participation because private companies (large bank holding companies and nonbank financial companies) send certified reports to a federal body. That reading fails the definition. These are mandatory supervisory disclosures that keep the Council "informed." They are not consultation, a comment period, a hearing, an advisory body, or a right to sue over a federal decision. The flow is one-way regulatory information-gathering, much like the defect notices in Example 11, and nothing here asks outsiders for their views before the Council decides something.

qwen_chat.w: This section requires financial institutions to submit reports to the Council for informational purposes. This is a regulatory reporting requirement, not a process where the government consults with or coordinates with outside parties to make a decision. The definition of participation involves consulting or coordinating with people outside the government before making a decision, which is not what is happening here; the companies are simply providing data.

qwen_chat.b:
Temptation: It looks like participation because it involves companies submitting reports to the government.
Resolution: Submitting reports or data to a federal agency is a regulatory compliance requirement, not a form of participation in decision-making. The definition explicitly excludes applications and implies that mere reporting is not consultation or coordination for the purpose of making a decision with outside input.
